I'm building a backtesting framework in R called ledgr. Naturally, I wanted
to know how it compares with other frameworks, so I measured it. That is how
I ended up being thoroughly humbled by Enrico Schumann's PMwR.

PMwR stands for Portfolio Management with R. It covers backtesting,
transactions, returns and portfolio analysis. Its backtesting engine,
`btest`, is written in R, and you can open the source and read the
simulation loop. [@pmwr-manual; @pmwr-source]

It is also ridiculously fast. It turned out to be one of the fastest backtesting engines I tested,
and on one workload it was the fastest by a wide margin.

vectorbt, the Python framework most people would name if you asked for a fast backtester,
was faster in my larger runs. Speed is one of its selling points, and the version I tested runs on a
Numba-compiled backend. PMwR was still within the same order of magnitude on those larger workloads,
and on a workload of many small independent backtests it won outright.

## Why I hadn't taken it seriously

I knew PMwR existed. My reasons for not taking it seriously don't
hold up very well now.

I'm used to software that announces its ambitions. vectorbt puts
"Blazing fast" and "the speed of C" on its front page. Performance is
central to its pitch, and my measurements give me no reason to object.
[@vectorbt]

PMwR describes itself as providing "reliable, efficient and convenient
tools." Having now measured it, "efficient" reads like academic
understatement. Competitive with vectorbt on these workloads is
considerably more than I would have inferred from that description.
[@pmwr-home]

That difference in presentation affected my judgment. I read the quiet
homepage and moved on. I had become accustomed to software marketing,
and academic understatement barely registered. That was a poor way to
judge the engineering. PMwR has public source repositories, a README and
extensive documentation; I simply hadn't given it a fair look.
[@pmwr-readme]

PMwR doesn't need a different personality. But I would have put those
timings on the front page.

## The benchmark

The data are synthetic, and the strategy is deliberately boring: a five-
and ten-period moving-average crossover rule, targeting either zero or one
share per instrument.

@tbl-warm-comparison reports warm timings from the October 31 baseline in
seconds, each the median of five completed repeats. The fastest time in
each row is in bold.


::: {#tbl-warm-comparison .cell tbl-cap='Warm elapsed seconds; median of five completed repeats per workflow.'}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|Workload                                                  |     PMwR| vectorbt| ledgr, durable|
|:---------------------------------------------------------|--------:|--------:|--------------:|
|10 instruments × 7,200 bars                         |     0.14| **0.08**|          10.68|
|1,166 instruments × 252 bars                        |     0.27| **0.14**|          11.31|
|20 instruments × 23,400 bars                        |     0.57| **0.25**|          45.81|
|100 independent runs, each 12 instruments × 90 bars | **0.50**|     2.43|          53.86|


:::
:::


The last row is 100 separate backtests rather than a parameter grid packed
into one vectorized call. One large simulation and many small ones stress
different parts of a framework. vectorbt handles the first case very well,
and PMwR turned out to be surprisingly strong at the second. Parameter-grid
throughput is a separate question.

PMwR and vectorbt matched exactly on portfolio state across all nine
qualification cases; their reported transaction prices differed.

<details id="benchmark-methodology">
<summary>Benchmark methodology</summary>

**Strategy and input.** Every portfolio starts flat with $10 million in
cash, with zero fees and slippage. Signals use the current close, and the
intended execution is the next bar's open. The first usable moving-average
pair seeds the rule; trading requires a later transition. Unknown signals
hold existing positions, and final-bar changes have no following bar on
which to fill. The data are synthetic and only there to exercise the
machinery.

**Warm clock.** Every experiment starts from already prepared native input,
creates a fresh book, recalculates indicators and materializes the required
results. Imports, CSV loading, reusable preparation and first-use
compilation are outside the warm clock. Experiment-specific setup remains
inside it.

**Versions and measurement date.** These measurements use PMwR 1.3-0, vectorbt 1.2.0 with its Numba engine
explicitly selected, and a frozen ledgr build, `891c23c8`. They describe the
October 31 baseline, before the new core discussed below.

**Scope.** This article shares the measured SMA workloads from an unfinished
peer-suite project. The archived report retains its original internal-review
and preliminary status. These observations do not establish a general
framework ranking or acceptance of the complete suite.

**Equivalence checks.** Timing comparisons are only useful if the frameworks do approximately the
same thing. My qualification checks covered nine cases, including every
workload in the table and a separate 500-instrument, 1,260-bar run. Cash,
equity, holdings and strategy decisions matched exactly between PMwR and
vectorbt in all nine cases. Reported transaction prices did not: the pinned
PMwR recipe writes closing prices to its journal while the wealth
calculation uses the open. The report keeps that discrepancy explicit, so
the claim I'm comfortable making is agreement on portfolio state.

</details>

The [full benchmark report](../../benchmarks/backtesting/2026-10-31/report.html)
includes cold timings, spread, other frameworks and memory observations.
[Methods, versions, hardware, downloadable data and the source bundle](../../benchmarks/backtesting/2026-10-31/index.qmd)
are available alongside it.

## ledgr's numbers

Yes, ledgr is in the table, and its measured durable workflows took roughly
40 to 110 times as long as the PMwR workflows on these workloads. These are
elapsed times for the completed workflows, including their different
persistence obligations.

Some of that gap is intentional. ledgr preserves a durable execution and
accounting history and reconstructs results from that history. The two
frameworks aren't trying to preserve the same amount of information.
I doubt that explains a 40- to 110-fold difference, though.

Profiling points to plenty of waste: list-based state, repeated copying,
repeated instrument lookups, per-step serialization, context construction,
and reconstructing accounting after the engine has finished. None of that
is the price of R; it's the price of how I wrote it.

## How plain R gets this fast

Reading PMwR's source gives some clues. Prices and portfolio histories live
in matrices, and cash and wealth are preallocated vectors. The simulation
steps through time with an ordinary R loop, while operations across
instruments use vector arithmetic. [@pmwr-source]

A loop over 20,000 time steps can be cheap if each iteration touches a few
preallocated vectors and matrix columns. The same loop gets expensive if
every step allocates lists, resolves names, copies objects, validates
structures and rebuilds state. What makes a backtester slow is what
happens inside the loop.

I can't tell from the source how much each design choice contributes. But
it gave me better questions to ask about my own code: how often am I
copying state, resolving names that could have been resolved once,
repeating work inside the hot loop, or re-validating something that was
already established? Those questions have been more useful than wondering
whether to rewrite everything in C++.

"Plain R" needs a qualification, of course. R's vector operations call
compiled native code, and R itself is not somehow executing on pure
thoughts and goodwill. My R recipes also use TTR for the moving averages;
its rolling calculations call compiled routines. It is PMwR's simulation
and accounting code that I'm describing as plain R. [@ttr-source]

The usual answer to "how do I make this fast" these days is a rewrite
in Rust or C++. vectorbt itself offers an optional Rust backend for
supported operations; these measurements use Numba. PMwR reaches these
timings without a PMwR-specific compiled simulation engine, which moved my
estimate of how fast an R backtester can get before compiled code becomes
the only option left. [@vectorbt-engines]

## Should I have started from PMwR?

This is the uncomfortable part. Knowing what I know now, the economically
better choice might have been to start from PMwR's engine and explore how
far it can be extended instead of writing another backtester from scratch.

ledgr exists because I wanted things that matter to my own research:
point-in-time data handling, explicit decision-time semantics, durable
experiment state, execution and accounting that can explain what
happened, and reproducible research objects that can be reopened later.
None of those obviously requires a slow simulation core. Some of them
certainly cost time, and some of PMwR's speed may come from doing less work
per step.

How much of ledgr's gap is the unavoidable price of those features and how
much is bad architecture, I don't know yet, but I can measure it. If I
remove the avoidable work and ledgr is still far behind, the uncomfortable
conclusion is also the useful one: I should probably have started from
PMwR.

## What's next

I'm currently working on ledgr v0.2.3. Most of the performance work comes
down to doing less: fewer allocations, fewer repeated lookups, more compact
typed state, and cheaper reconstruction after simulation. Some of that was
already planned, and PMwR gave me a much less comfortable target. I'll rerun
the same benchmark against the new core and publish the result, including
the numbers that make ledgr look bad.

In the meantime, if you want a fast backtester in R, it already exists.
Enrico Schumann built it, and it deserves far more attention than its
homepage asks for.
